meta.method: Events at indices 0-74 (na-e-001 to na-e-075). Fetched all 124 cited pages afresh (Wikipedia through its parse API, slowly, identifying by https://atlasforatlas.com) and read past each quote in the full text, including infoboxes and footnote lists, to trace credited authors. Checked statement, title, date, place and every FIELD note. Went outside the cited pages by search where a figure, date or founder looked wrong (El Anil and Buatachive, the founding of Merida, Anza's force, the Cypress Hills toll). Rules applied: tolls and army sizes need a named giver, except a side's count of its own dead; vague 'one account' counts as unnamed. Could not open: The Canadian Encyclopedia (403; Wayback refused to this fetcher), the Library of Congress post cited by Wikipedia for the Long Walk numbers (found its address, did not read the figure), and no printed book was read.

na-e-001.note: All supported. Aztec_Triple_Alliance has 1428 in the infobox and 1430 in the narrative; the card gives both. The date is before the catalogue's 1492 window, as background; an earlier round passed it.

na-e-002.note: date.day: 18 September is one author's date for entering the capital, not the alliance, as the card's own note admits. Wikipedia's Spanish_conquest_of_the_Aztec_Empire, cited on the next card, says Cortes arrived on 23 September 1519 and stayed twenty days; its timeline has Tlaxcallan brokering peace after 18 days of war. Fix: date to month precision (September 1519) and give both entry dates or neither. Schmal's 'king' is attributed, but Tlaxcallan cites it as a confederation with several rulers.

na-e-003.note: Named figures all on the page. Date conflict is real (infobox 30 June to 1 July) and the note records it. Chroniclers known through Wikipedia.

na-e-004.note: Alchon confirmed as footnote 4 on the mortality sentence, book not read. Note is right that this page says Cuitlahuac died of smallpox flatly while his own article says perhaps; the card takes the weaker.

na-e-005.note: Bjornson and Jonassohn confirmed as footnote 7 on 100,000, book not read. Schmal's 'Aztec historians' are unnamed by him: a weak credit, but correctly worded as a report. Infobox also lists 100,000 killed in action separately under another footnote.

na-e-006.note: statement: misreads the source. In Tangaxuan_II the one who allied with Don Pedro Panza is Guzman, against the Cazonci; the card reads as if Tangaxuan were allied with him, which turns the betrayal around. Fix: 'Guzman ... found him still de facto ruler, and allied himself with a Purepecha noble, Don Pedro Panza Cuinierangari, against him.' FIELD place: confirmed wrong. Nothing places the execution at Tzintzuntzan; infobox has Nueva Galicia, and the same page says his ashes went into the Lerma river, a line the card omits. Fix: approximate true and relabel as the Purepecha capital standing for the event, or move to the Rio Lerma (Executed Today says the Lerma-Angulo confluence; a weak source, so not as a precise point).

na-e-007.note: Statement supported, including Alvarado at Mixton per the page. place: Nochistlan is Tenamaztle's home, not where the rising began; no page read locates the start. Fix: approximate true. Gerhard's words reach the card through a footnote quoting Schmal, as the note says.

na-e-008.note: statement: the founder. The cited article's 'he founded' follows a sentence about Montejo's cousin, and the card took that as the cousin founding Merida. Wikipedia's Francisco de Montejo the Younger and Merida articles and Mexican press credit Montejo the Younger (el Mozo). Fix: 'the Spanish under Francisco de Montejo the Younger founded the colonial town of Merida', or state the disagreement. The Tutul-Xiu material is supported.

na-e-009.note: statement attribution: 5 to 15 million and 800,000 are unnamed on the card although the footnotes are traceable. Fix: 'Acuna-Soto and colleagues estimate 5 to 15 million', 'Warinner and colleagues about 800,000' (footnotes 2 and 26; papers not read). participants: caxcan unsupported, as an earlier round found. place: a single Tenochtitlan point stands for a wide epidemic, so approximate true.

na-e-010.note: Supported. The page says supply routes 'of Purepecha'; the card's plain 'supply routes' is not wrong, and Spanish colonies were attacked days later. Infobox records a Chichimeca victory, not on the card; optional.

na-e-011.note: Gradie p.1 confirmed as footnote 14 on the toll; book not read. All else supported.

na-e-012.note: Follows Tarahumara closely; single source, as the note says.

na-e-013.note: Jones 2009 p.59 confirmed as footnote 17 (with Schwartz 1990 as 18). 13 March is the detailed account in the main article, which has the waterborne assault that morning, so the stored date stands over Nojpeten's 10 March. 'Last independent native kingdom in the Americas' is the source's wording.

na-e-014.note: statement: the Tepich killings are given one way. Wikipedia has Chi ordering all non-Maya killed; Yucatan Today, also cited and the source of the 'widely considered' start, says he killed several white families. Fix: give both, attributed. participants: cruzob did not exist yet in 1847, and an earlier round flagged this.

na-e-015.note: date.day and statement: Wikipedia probably merges two fights. The Texas Band of Yaqui Indians' history (tbyi.gov/history) says El Anil fell on 5 May 1886, and that 12 May was Buatachive, where General Martinez's troops killed 200 Yaquis in a three-hour battle and captured hundreds of women and children while Cajeme and a couple of thousand escaped. A Sonoran government history found by search also gives 5 May. The card's own Encyclopedia.com citation names Buatachive, about four thousand captured. Fix: date El Anil 5 May, or month precision with the conflict stated, and credit the 12 May and 200 dead to Buatachive. Read Troncoso (1905) if possible. Credit him as Francisco P. Troncoso, as the page's bibliography does; 'del Paso y Troncoso' suggests a different, better-known scholar.

na-e-016.note: statement attribution: 600 Zuni warriors and the 230 horse and 70 foot carry only 'by one account', with no author; the note admits the footnote was not traced. They also sit oddly beside na-e-007, where Coronado takes more than 1,600 north: these figures can only be a part of the force. Fix: name the giver or drop the 600, and say 'an advance force' if a source supports that. No Zuni account read, as noted.

na-e-017.note: statement: 'first capital until 1610' compresses too far. The page says it became the first capital and separately that the capital moved to Santa Fe in 1610; the Onate article's own reference list names San Gabriel de Yunque-Ouinge, the seat most histories put between them. Fix: 'the first capital; the capital moved to Santa Fe in 1610'. FIELD date: confirmed, day available. Fix: 11 July 1598 at day precision, or 12 July if the event is the renaming.

na-e-018.note: statement attribution: 'One account counts about 800' is an unnamed Wikipedia estimate (500 men, 300 women and children). NPS's 1,500 is named. Fix: trace the giver or drop the 800. No Acoma account was read and the cited detail looks to come from the Spanish side, so the card should say so once that is checked. The rest, including 'reportedly' on the seizure of food, is supported.

na-e-019.note: statement attribution: 'about 400' killed has no named giver. Fix: name it after tracing Pueblo_Revolt footnotes 21-22, or write 'Spanish losses are put at about 400'. Rest supported; the plan date of 11 August versus 13 August is in the note. Besieged Santa Fe is on both pages though not quoted.

na-e-020.note: statement attribution: 70 executed is credited on Diego_de_Vargas to the historian Enrique Lamadrid, and the card does not say so. 'By one account' for sixty soldiers is also unnamed. Fix: 'by Enrique Lamadrid's account, 70 ...', and note that the Vargas article gives about 100 soldiers on the 1693 return. 14 September stands as the catalogue date against 12 September in the Vargas article.

na-e-021.note: statement: 'killed all the men' is stated flat, but the account rests on Hopi tradition; Awatovi's footnotes run to Malotki's Hopi Tales of Destruction and neither source gives a toll. EBSCO says 'about the year 1700'. Fix: 'In Hopi tradition, as recorded by Malotki, the attackers killed the men ...' and date as circa. Check Malotki directly if available.

na-e-022.note: statement: the main article has Bent left alive, escaping through the wall into the house next door, and killed there, so 'at his house' follows the compressed Taos_Pueblo line. Fix: 'killed Governor Charles Bent in Taos'. Garrard: footnote 6 confirmed, but the page presents him as eyewitness of the trials, not the church fight, so the note's 'eyewitness' is too strong; infobox has about 367 rebels killed overall. Fix: keep the credit, say 'memoir' and drop eyewitness. participants: mexico unsupported, as an earlier round found.

na-e-023.note: All supported. Note's 1853 versus 1854 point is right.

na-e-024.note: Supported. Tohono O'odham page adds that the O'odham were not informed of the purchase, which directly supports the line an earlier draft dropped; worth restoring with that citation.

na-e-025.note: Supported. 'Captured teamsters' compresses nine Mexicans tortured and killed and three Americans killed later on the flight to Sonora. Date could sharpen, the meeting being in early February.

na-e-026.note: statement attribution: 'The Apache claimed 63' overstates it. The page says Capt. Cremony reported a prominent unnamed Apache as saying 63 were killed by artillery; the note says uncredited, but the page names him. Infobox footnote is Clodfelter (2017). Fix: 'Capt. John Cremony later quoted an unnamed Apache who put 63 killed by artillery.' The 500 is 'other accounts' and unnamed.

na-e-027.note: Jan 1864 on EBSCO, which agrees on 23 killed, adds 200 surrendered and at least 200 head seized; Canyon_de_Chelly's 1863 is an outlier. No Dine account read.

na-e-028.note: statement attribution: misattributed. On Long_Walk_of_the_Navajo the 10,000 and 500 sentence carries footnote 2, a Library of Congress blog post (In Custodia Legis, 18 June 2018), not Jaimes; Jaimes is footnote 1, on the return in 1868 and with 2 on the infobox's 2,500 to 3,500. The note repeats the error. Up to 3,500 has no marker of its own. Fix: read blogs.loc.gov/law/2018/06/naaltsoos-sn-and-the-long-walk-home/ and credit it, or say 'The Library of Congress's law blog is the source Wikipedia gives'; give the range 2,500 to 3,500; keep EBSCO's 6,000 for March 1864. EBSCO also reports Navajo oral tradition of killings on the march, which would balance the card.

na-e-029.note: statement: 'in one reading' hides a named disagreement on the same page. Historian Jennifer Nez Denetdale calls the treaty the point at which the Navajo lost freedom and autonomy and came under American colonial rule. Fix: give her reading beside the sovereignty one. All else supported.

na-e-030.note: statement attribution: 144 has no named giver. Page footnotes Konstantin (popular reference) on 144 and Jacoby 2009 on the children. Fix: check Jacoby's Shadows at Dawn for the count and credit it; the page has Whitman burying the dead but does not say he counted them. The page's point that the O'odham were the main fighters and had lost livestock to Apache raids is left off, and the note holds it; the card could carry it for balance.

na-e-031.note: Statement supported, attributed to the Southern Ute Tribe. FIELD place confirmed: signing at Los Pinos Agency, the point is the ceded mountains. Fix: approximate true and keep the point, since the title is about the land.

na-e-032.note: statement: contested framing given one way. The card says the Utes 'ambushed the column', while the cited Newsline page says they had been promised no troops would enter the reservation and quotes historian Charles Marsh on a force bearing down on a peaceful encampment, with Sand Creek in memory. The card leaves all that in the note. Fix: add the promise and Marsh, attributed, and give Newsline's about two dozen dead on each side.

na-e-033.note: Supported. FIELD date confirmed: fix to 30 August 1881, day precision. Page carries a needs-citations banner.

na-e-034.note: Supported on both pages, including the train from Fort Bowie and Fort Pickens.

na-e-035.note: Supported. NPS has Anza at Yuma in January 1774. 'Damaged' against 'destroyed' is handled in the note.

na-e-036.note: Supported. 'Pressed' softens the page's terms, under which the Mohave would otherwise be destroyed, and the Battle of the Colorado River is omitted; both optional. Year 1858 and a point at a fort of 1859 are fine for the war as a whole.

na-e-037.note: Homer Davidson confirmed as footnote 9 for about 250. Both framings present; the third on the page, that the Apache taunted Davidson into attacking, is optional.

na-e-038.note: place: the point is Fort Laramie, 30 miles from the mouth of Horse Creek, yet approximate is false; the name also carries research language ('point shown is Fort Laramie'). Fix: approximate true, or Wikidata coordinates for the mouth of Horse Creek, and name it simply 'Mouth of Horse Creek'. Statement supported.

na-e-039.note: place: same defect. Wikipedia's infobox gives the site, 42.13222, -104.40583, against the stored fort. Fix: use a Wikidata or marker coordinate, drop 'point shown' from the name. statement: 29 on the lead against 31 in the infobox, single source; say 'about 30' or give both.

na-e-040.note: Supported. MNopedia says a six-week conflict, Wikipedia five weeks; 'about five weeks by one account' is fine, though 'five or six weeks' is better.

na-e-041.note: kind: war.massacre is wrong for the title's mass execution. Fix: state.execution, as na-e-068. Add 'in US history' for 'the nation's history'. Statement otherwise supported.

na-e-042.note: statement attribution: 'most sources estimate around 150' is summary wording and the page names givers. Fix: 'Alan Brinkley gives 133, of whom 105 women and children; the eyewitness John Smith 70 to 80; the Park Service at least 150.' Chivington's claim stays. Rest supported.

na-e-043.note: Supported, including Crow land and no Crow consent. White Elk, a Cheyenne, is the named source for the ten decoys if a name is wanted.

na-e-044.note: Supported. The source's 1901 for Lone Wolf is its error (decided 1903), and the card rightly omits the year; correct the note.

na-e-045.note: Supported. Court's reading of the three-fourths clause is the right one to use over North Dakota Studies'.

na-e-046.note: Supported; the card separates military from Cheyenne figures, and NPS confirms Black Kettle survived Sand Creek.

na-e-048.note: statement: one-sided toll. Gives US dead only, 'by one count' with no name, and leaves off the infobox's 31 to 100 Native dead and 10 non-combatants for want of an author. Fix: give both from the same infobox or neither; the same standard should apply to both sides. Date of 25 June is the day of Custer's fight; fine.

na-e-049.note: Statement supported on the Court's text. kind: state.treaty is wrong for an act of Congress enforcing a disputed agreement. Fix: a legal or annexation kind. place: Black Hills centre at round coordinates, approximate should be true.

na-e-050.note: statement attribution: 'another account gives 250 to 300' is unnamed. Wikipedia's notes derive the upper figure from Nelson Miles's report of some 300 snow-covered forms; the 146 is the commonly cited trench burial. HISTORY.com is a thin credit for a much-researched toll. Fix: read Utley or Ostler from the page's notes, or say 'the army buried 146 in a mass grave; Gen. Miles reported some 300 bodies', after a check. Rest supported.

na-e-051.note: statement attribution: 'are said to have died' can be named: footnote 2 is James Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013), and the page also has the 1839 Commissioner of Indian Affairs using 17,200 and thinking the wider toll double. Chardon: the same page quotes him writing 'twenty-three', with accounts of 23, 27 or 138, so 'twenty-seven' alone picks one. Fix: give the range and credit Daschuk and the Commissioner.

na-e-052.note: statement: force size. 'With Ute and Apache allies and about 800 Spanish soldiers' follows one Wikipedia sentence, unnamed. Other accounts have about 600 Spanish joined by about 200 Ute and Apache, which makes 800 the total (Manitou Springs Heritage Center, Palmer Lake Historical Society; Wikipedia's Cuerno Verde says 500 to 800 mixed). Fix: 'a force of about 800 with Ute and Apache allies'. Thomas (1932), footnoted, prints Anza's diary. No Comanche account read.

na-e-053.note: Supported. Note's 'earlier note 353' is in fact the page's own figure; correct the note. Size varies 297 to 353; about 300 stands.

na-e-054.note: statement attribution: 'By some estimates nearly 158' is the Oklahoma Historical Society's own vagueness and should be credited to it. Fix: 'The Oklahoma Historical Society reports estimates of nearly 158 ...'. Rest supported.

na-e-055.note: Supported from DCB, named. Wikipedia also calls it the Seven Oaks Massacre; the note has it.

na-e-056.note: statement: DCB, the card's main source, says Peguis later called the tobacco a goodwill token and that no formal surrender had taken place; the card stops at illegal settlement. It also treats the strip as the whole grant, where DCB says it included plots of six miles round Forts Douglas and Daer and Grand Forks. Fix: add Peguis's protest and 'included'. place: Fort Garry was not built by 1817; DCB's post is Fort Douglas. Fix: name it The Forks, approximate true.

na-e-057.note: Statement supported and well attributed. place: Prince of Wales Fort is not in the source, which names only Hudson's Bay Company posts and western Canada. Fix: approximate true.

na-e-058.note: statement attribution: 'eventually 6,000 died' has no author on the card or in Wikipedia's sentence. Fix: trace a giver or drop the figure; Payne gives none. Overlap with na-e-051 is real but each covers different nations.

na-e-059.note: statement attribution: the range has named ends. Baker's official report claimed 173, while scout Joe Kipp later said 217 (via Blackfoot Digital Library and Graybill). Fix: 'Baker reported 173; his scout Joe Kipp later said 217.' Page also holds survivor accounts (Spear Woman, Bear Head) worth citing. Rest supported.

na-e-060.note: Supported, with both readings of the cession.

na-e-061.note: statement: one-sided toll. 'Accounts differ' then gives only 13, from a man travelling with the attackers. Search found The Canadian Encyclopedia at least 20; Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan nearly 30; Office of the Treaty Commissioner about 20 by some historians and closer to 300 by survivors. Fix: give that range, attributed. Also the party was led by Hardwick and John Evans and included Metis freighters; 'wolfers' alone is short. Participants lists only assiniboine.

na-e-062.note: Supported. Note is wrong that Fort Walsh could not be re-read: the cited Treaty_4 page lists the Fort Walsh adhesion by Stony and Assiniboine bands on 25 September 1877 and first signers as Cree, Saulteaux and Assiniboine. Add that to the card and fix the note, which also answers the Assiniboine in participants.

na-e-063.note: Supported. Page has signings 23 and 28 August and 9 September in the infobox, and 18 August as the start of negotiation; stored date stands.

na-e-064.note: statement: the cause and the framing. The page does not say the pressing for a written text is why the nations may have been misinformed, only sets the two side by side, and it is an unattributed Wikipedia aside. The Blackfoot understanding is the contested point of this treaty and is absent. Fix: drop 'Because', and restore a Blackfoot-side account from The True Spirit and Original Intent of Treaty 7 or a Canadian Encyclopedia Wayback copy.

na-e-065.note: statement: the eight hanged were not all for Frog Lake: the page says the trials covered Frog Lake and the Battleford killings of Payne and Tremont, without counsel. DCB also names Big Bear's son Ayimisis as a leader. Fix: 'Wandering Spirit and seven others, some for killings at Battleford, were hanged ...'. Rest supported.

na-e-066.note: statement attribution: 392 is unnamed and the same page's infobox says 350; the note knows. Fix: 'about 350 to 392 men'. Rest supported, including Dewdney's leave.

na-e-067.note: Both tolls named on the card. Note's chain is confirmed: Middleton footnote is a New York Times report, Vegreville's first footnote the Panet report. Metis strength of 250 is available if wanted.

na-e-069.note: title and date: assent on 12 May did not itself admit Manitoba; the page gives commencement on 15 July 1870. Fix: title 'Manitoba Act receives royal assent', or date the admission 15 July. FIELD place confirmed: passed at Ottawa, point is Red River. Fix: approximate true. Statement supported.

na-e-070.note: Supported. 'Peace and friendship' is correctly attributed to the Treaty 8 page. Place point is the lake, about 45 km from Grouard where the page puts the signing; set approximate true.

na-e-071.note: title: DCB says an alliance 'is suggested', so 'alliance' in the title is stronger than the text, and it names Algonkins and Etchemins as well as Innu. Fix: 'Champlain and Anadabijou at Tadoussac: alliance proposed'. FIELD date confirmed: fix to 27 May 1603, day precision. Statement supported.

na-e-072.note: FIELD date confirmed wrong: 1142 is a single proposal stored as the date. statement: read past the infobox quote. The cited Iroquois page says many archaeologists and anthropologists put it about 1450 and elsewhere likely between 1142 and 1660, with little agreement. The card leaves out the mainstream view and takes 1450 as an upper limit. The note says 1142 came through The Canadian Encyclopedia, yet this page gives the eclipse of 31 August 1142 itself. Fix: date as a range, 1142 to 1660 circa, and add 'many archaeologists say about 1450'. Date is outside the catalogue's window.

na-e-073.note: statement: the card's own Tuscarora_War citation dates the war to February 1715, against 1711 to 1713. Fix: '1711 to 1715'. place: nothing read places the admission at Onondaga, and the sponsor was the Oneida. Fix: approximate true. 1722 and the rest supported.

na-e-074.note: place: Montreal is a stand-in and approximate is false; it also did not exist in 1609. The start is Champlain's fight at Ticonderoga, July 1609, on the same page. Fix: move the point to the Ticonderoga fight with month precision, or keep Montreal with approximate true and date the card as a range to 1701. Statement supported.

na-e-075.note: Supported. The card avoids the source's anachronistic Six Nations. 39 against over 40 nations is in the note.
